h1: Bramling Cross hops and their blackcurrant note in ales
title: Bramling Cross Hops and Blackcurrant | Craft Beer School
desc: Bramling Cross hops explained: where the blackcurrant note comes from, typical alpha, how much to use late and the ales it suits best.
teaser: An English hop with a Canadian wild parent. That is where the blackcurrant comes from.
standfirst: Bramling Cross is the English hop that tastes of blackcurrant and lemon. It is old, a little odd and very useful in dark and fruity ales. Here is how to get the fruit without the harshness.
sections: A Golding crossed with a wild Canadian hop

Bramling Cross was bred at Wye College in Kent in 1927. The breeder, Professor E. S. Salmon, crossed Bramling, an old Golding type, with a wild hop from Manitoba in Canada. The seedling took more than two decades to reach commercial gardens and was released in the 1950s.

That wild North American parent is the reason Bramling Cross does not taste like a typical English hop. Where Fuggle is earthy and Goldings are honeyed and floral, Bramling Cross brings blackcurrant, loganberry and lemon, with a spicy finish. Alpha acid is moderate, usually 5 to 8%.

Boil it for an hour and the fruit mostly goes. Bittering with Bramling Cross gives a fairly ordinary, slightly coarse bitterness. The character lives in the oils, which are volatile and boil away fast.

So the fruit comes from late use:

  • Additions in the last 10 minutes of the boil.
  • A whirlpool or hop stand at 75 to 80 °C for 20 minutes.
  • A dry hop at 2 to 3 g per litre after primary fermentation has slowed.

For a 20 litre batch, 30 g at flameout and 40 to 60 g as a dry hop is a sensible starting point. Taste it at bottling. Push the dose higher next time if the blackcurrant is too shy.

Bramling Cross works best where there is enough malt to frame the fruit:

  • Best bitters with a little crystal malt, where blackcurrant sits on caramel.
  • Porters and stouts. Dark fruit and roast make a natural pair.
  • Winter and Christmas ales, where it plays with dried fruit and spice notes.
  • Golden ales, if you want something fruitier than Goldings but still English.

It is a harder fit in a crisp lager, where the coarse edge and berry notes feel out of place. Our guide to English hops sets it beside the rest of the family.
A homebrew porter that shows it off

Here is a 20 litre porter at about OG 1.050:

  • Maris Otter pale malt 3.8 kg (80%).
  • Brown malt 0.48 kg (10%).
  • Crystal malt around 150 EBC 0.29 kg (6%).
  • Chocolate malt 0.19 kg (4%).
  • Challenger or Northdown at 60 minutes for about 25 IBU.
  • Bramling Cross 30 g at flameout, 40 g dry hop.

Ferment with an English ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. The roast holds up the blackcurrant. The bittering hop does the dull job so Bramling Cross can do the interesting one.
Getting the fruit without the harshness

The common complaint about Bramling Cross is a rough, almost catty edge. Two habits help. First, keep it out of the long boil and bitter with something smoother. Second, keep dry hop contact short. Three to four days at fermentation temperature extracts most of the aroma. A fortnight on the hops pulls out more grassy and vegetal flavour.

The detail that matters most at home is temperature. Dry hopping at 18 to 20 °C extracts aroma well. Dry hopping a beer that has warmed to 28 °C on a Mumbai balcony pulls harsh, green flavours faster. If you cannot control temperature, dry hop for less time.
Buying and storing it in India

Bramling Cross is a small English crop and not always in stock with Indian homebrew suppliers. Buy it in sealed foil packs, check the harvest year and keep it in the freezer. Aroma hops lose their character faster than they lose alpha acid, so an old pack can still bitter but may have lost the blackcurrant you paid for.

If you cannot find it, there is no perfect swap. A blend of Goldings with a small amount of a berry-leaning hop gets close. That is the honest answer: some hops are worth hunting for.

Bramling Cross does not have to work alone. Two blends work well at home. Pair it with Goldings late in the boil for a classic English base with a berry top note, roughly two parts Goldings to one part Bramling Cross. Or pair it with Southern Cross for a brighter, lemon-led pale ale where the blackcurrant sits underneath.

Keep the total late hop weight the same as a single hop recipe and split it. That way you change one thing at a time. Write the ratio on the bottle cap or the label so you can tell batches apart when you taste them side by side a month later. Memory is a poor lab notebook.
Why the same hop tastes different every year

Hop oil levels move with each harvest, so one year's Bramling Cross can be noticeably fruitier than the next. Explaining that swing and correcting a recipe for it needs an understanding of hop oils and how they survive boiling, whirlpool and fermentation. That chemistry is what turns a recipe follower into a brewer who can predict a result.
faqs: What does Bramling Cross taste like?
Blackcurrant, loganberry and lemon, with some spice. The fruit comes through in late additions and dry hopping rather than in the bittering.
Is Bramling Cross good for bittering?
It can bitter, but the result is ordinary and slightly coarse. Most brewers bitter with another hop and save Bramling Cross for late additions.
Best bitters, porters, stouts and winter ales are the usual homes. The dark fruit character suits malt-led beers.
